source.title: Convexifying Transformers: Improving optimization and understanding of transformer networks
source.authors: Tolga Ergen; Behnam Neyshabur; Harsh Mehta

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares test performance of a convex alternative attention model with standard nonconvex attention, but it does not test any listed version's specific intervention or measure.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports modular-division test accuracy and loss, but those synthetic algorithmic-task results do not test the claim about natural data. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study compares proposed convex attention training with nonconvex attention training. Its experiments and theoretical arguments do not test any of V1–V8. Both approaches use Adam; no optimizer comparison is performed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report improved optimization and test performance, derive a token-sparsity interpretation, and report reduced grokking delays. They explicitly limit empirical validation to a few small-scale instances and call for larger-scale verification.
record.recipe_differences: Replaces standard self-attention with a convex attention formulation; the paper compares this approach with standard nonconvex training.

fits_no_version.finding: In the BERT sixth-layer student-teacher experiment using MRPC inputs, the proposed convex model obtains lower test loss than standard nonconvex attention training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Convex attention training can improve held-out activation prediction relative to standard nonconvex attention training in this student-teacher setting.

fits_no_version.finding: On modular-division tasks, the proposed approach reaches high test accuracy faster and reduces the delay between fitting training data and generalizing. Depth also improves some results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed attention formulation reduces grokking delays in the tested modular-division settings.

record.problems: The authors describe their empirical validation as limited to a few small-scale problem instances. The BERT test-loss comparison is presented in a figure without numeric values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Modular-division test accuracy and loss in Figures 4–7 were left out because they concern synthetic algorithmic tasks rather than natural-data generalization. No other in-scope results were omitted.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label memorization and natural-label generalization, including chance performance on held-out random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning dependence, and optimizer or weight-decay remedies.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout's effects across training-set sizes and its interaction with augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations, and comparisons with other measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: T4 does not apply: the study does not use any listed version as a tool. Synthetic tasks are outside these versions because they lack the specified interventions and comparisons; synthetic data alone is not a general exclusion rule. The appendix's width threshold establishes optimization equivalence, not decreasing test error with width.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error across widths beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Effects of dropout and its removal with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
